```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5, dpi = 110)
library(cpueTargeting)
library(ggplot2)
# Results: loaded from rdata/ if pre-run (inst/scripts/run_tuna_flat.R and
# run_tuna_contrast.R); otherwise computed here if
# options(cpueTargeting.run_vignettes = TRUE), else the code is only shown.
rdata <- getOption("cpueTargeting.rdata", "../rdata")
files <- file.path(rdata, c("tuna_flat_single.rds", "tuna_contrast_single.rds",
                            "tuna_flat_replicates.rds", "tuna_contrast_replicates.rds"))
names(files) <- c("flat", "contrast", "flat_reps", "contrast_reps")
have_single <- all(file.exists(files[c("flat", "contrast")])) ||
  isTRUE(getOption("cpueTargeting.run_vignettes", FALSE))
have_reps <- all(file.exists(files[c("flat_reps", "contrast_reps")]))
```

In a tuna longline fishery, skippers target species not only through *where*
they fish but also through *how deep* they set their hooks, which depends on
the number of hooks between floats (HBF) and on the depth of the thermocline.
This vignette compares the standardisation methods in two scenarios with
**identical targeting** that differ only in the true trends:

| Scenario | Stocks | True trends |
|---|---|---|
| **Flat** | unfished at the start, lightly fished (`q = 0.2`, `B_start = 1`) | nearly flat |
| **Contrasting** | partly fished at the start, fished harder (package defaults) | diverging between species: BFT recovers, BET declines, ... |

With flat trends, every change in the catch composition is caused by
targeting. With contrasting trends, the composition also changes because the
species' relative abundances change.

Positions are reported as 5 x 5 blocks: logbooks rarely report positions at
the scale at which fish and fleets interact, and a longline set may span a
front. The thermocline moves between years in the results shown here
(`Moving`); results for a fixed thermocline are in the replicates.

# Settings

```{r settings}
prices <- matrix(c(rep(c(0.3, 0.2, 1.0, 2.0), 10),   # years 1-10: ALB (+ BFT)
                   rep(c(1.5, 2.5, 0.7, 0.3), 10),   # years 11-20: BET (+ YFT)
                   rep(c(1.0, 2.0, 1.5, 0.5), 10)),  # years 21-30: BET / BFT
                 ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE)             # columns: YFT, BET, BFT, ALB
contrast_settings <- tuna_settings()
contrast_settings$price <- prices
flat_settings <- modifyList(contrast_settings, list(q = 0.2, B_start = rep(1, 4)))
moving <- list(thermocline_annual_sd = 15, thermocline_annual_field_sd = 10)

with_thermocline <- function(s) list(Fixed = s, Moving = modifyList(s, moving))

models <- c("Base", "Base+S", "Cluster+S", "DPC+S", "HBF+S")

# Standardisation: 5 models, plus DPC+S with 2 PCs
fit_one <- function(sim) {
  fit <- standardize_cpue(sim, models = models, spatial_res = 5, n_pc = 3,
                          engine = "bam")
  fit_2pc <- standardize_cpue(sim, models = "DPC+S", n_pc = 2,
                              label = " (2 PCs)", engine = "bam")
  bind_comparisons(fit, fit_2pc)
}
# One scenario: simulations and fits for a fixed and a moving thermocline
run_single <- function(s, seed = 123) {
  sims <- lapply(with_thermocline(s), simulate_tuna, seed = seed, plots = FALSE)
  list(sims = sims, fits = lapply(sims, fit_one))
}
```

`flat` and `contrast` each hold `sims` and `fits` for the `Fixed` and `Moving`
thermocline, e.g. `flat$sims$Moving` and `flat$fits$Moving`. The pre-run results
from `inst/scripts/run_tuna_flat.R` and `run_tuna_contrast.R` are exactly
these objects:

```{r run, eval = FALSE}
flat <- run_single(flat_settings)
contrast <- run_single(contrast_settings)
```

```{r load, include = FALSE, eval = have_single}
# Pre-run results if available, otherwise the code above
if (all(file.exists(files[c("flat", "contrast")]))) {
  flat <- readRDS(files[["flat"]])
  contrast <- readRDS(files[["contrast"]])
} else {
  flat <- run_single(flat_settings)
  contrast <- run_single(contrast_settings)
}
```

The prices switch the fleet from the cool south (ALB) to the warm north (BET)
in year 11, which changes both where and how deep it fishes, and split it
between BET in the north and BFT in the south in year 21, which changes only
where it fishes.

```{r vertical, fig.height = 6}
plot_tuna_vertical_distributions()
```

# Nominal CPUE versus the truth

```{r nominal, eval = have_single}
plot_om(flat$sims$Moving)$CPUE + ggtitle("Flat true trends")
plot_om(contrast$sims$Moving)$CPUE + ggtitle("Contrasting true trends")
```

The same targeting produces jumps in nominal CPUE at years 11 and 21 in both
scenarios; only the true trends (blue) differ.

# Standardised indices

All models are Tweedie GAMs with `year` plus a targeting term (`+S`: spatial
smoother on the 5 x 5 blocks): Base (none), Cluster (4 clusters of the catch
composition), DPC (3 principal components, and 2 for comparison) and HBF (a
factor for the gear).


```{r indices, eval = have_single, fig.height = 7}
fits <- list(Flat = flat$fits$Moving, Contrasting = contrast$fits$Moving)
plot_indices(fits, models = models)
```

```{r index trends, eval = have_single, fig.height = 7}

plot_indices(fits, models = models, type = "points+smooth")
```

```{r rmse, eval = have_single}
plot_diagnostics(fits)
```

# What do the PCs capture?

```{r pcs, eval = have_single}
pp <- plot_pcs(flat$fits$Moving, pcs = c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3"))
pp$space
pp$depth
pp$time
```

PC1 is the north-south gradient (where), PC2 the depth of the hooks (how
deep): the PCA separates spatial and vertical targeting without being told
that depth exists. With flat trends, the PCs change only in steps at the
price switches. With contrasting trends, a gradual drift is added as the
species' relative abundances change:

```{r pcs-contrast, eval = have_single}
plot_pcs(contrast$fits$Moving, pcs = c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3"))$time
```

# What do the clusters capture?

```{r clusters, eval = have_single}
pc <- plot_clusters(flat$fits$Moving, switch_years = c(10.5, 20.5))
pc$composition
pc$time
pc$depth
pc$pca
```

# Replicates: flat versus contrasting trends

20 seeds of each scenario, with a fixed and a moving thermocline
(`inst/scripts/run_tuna_flat.R` and `run_tuna_contrast.R`):

```{r replicates, eval = have_reps, fig.height = 7}
reps <- rbind(
  data.frame(readRDS(files[["flat_reps"]])$diagnostics, trend = "Flat trends"),
  data.frame(readRDS(files[["contrast_reps"]])$diagnostics, trend = "Contrasting trends"))
reps$trend <- factor(reps$trend, levels = c("Flat trends", "Contrasting trends"))
reps$model <- factor(reps$model, levels = unique(as.character(reps$model)))

ggplot(reps, aes(x = model, y = rmse_log, fill = trend)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.6) +
  facet_grid(species ~ scenario, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "RMSE of log index", fill = NULL,
       title = "Same targeting: flat versus contrasting true trends") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), legend.position = "bottom")
```

# What to take from this

* **Space fixes *where*, not *how deep*.** The spatial term removes much of
  the bias from the north-south switches, but not the vertical targeting of
  BET.
* **HBF works only while the depth of the fish is stable.** With a moving
  thermocline, the same HBF fishes at different depths relative to the fish
  each year.
* **The catch composition captures both**, because it reflects where and how
  deep each set actually fished. With flat trends, DPC is close to the truth
  for all species.
* **But the catch composition also carries abundance.** When species'
  relative abundances change persistently, the PCs absorb part of the real
  trend of the species whose relative abundance changes most, and more PCs
  absorb more. Coarser, discrete clusters are less affected.
* Plotting the PCs over time helps to tell the two apart: targeting changes
  are steps at known changes in the fishery, abundance changes are gradual.
